```{python}
#| echo: false

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick
import seaborn as sns
from completejourney_py import get_data

cj = get_data()
transactions  = cj['transactions']
products      = cj['products']
demographics  = cj['demographics']

# Basket-level table — the backbone of the Part 2 worked example
baskets = (
    transactions
    .groupby(['household_id', 'basket_id'], as_index=False)
    .agg(basket_spend=('sales_value', 'sum'),
         coupon_disc=('coupon_disc', 'sum'),
         n_lines=('product_id', 'size'))
)
baskets['used_coupon']    = baskets['coupon_disc'] != 0
baskets['spend_per_line'] = baskets['basket_spend'] / baskets['n_lines']

# Joined to demographics (note: not every household has demographics)
baskets_demo = baskets.merge(demographics, on='household_id', how='inner')

# Simpler views used in Part 1 and Exercise 1
basket_spend = baskets[['household_id', 'basket_id', 'basket_spend']]
basket_demo  = baskets_demo

# Weekly sales
weekly_sales = (
    transactions
    .set_index('transaction_timestamp')['sales_value']
    .resample('W').sum()
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={'transaction_timestamp': 'week', 'sales_value': 'total_sales'})
)

# Top 10 departments by revenue
category_totals = (
    transactions
    .merge(products[['product_id', 'department']], on='product_id')
    .groupby('department', as_index=False)['sales_value'].sum()
    .sort_values('sales_value')
    .tail(10)
)

income_order = [
    'Under 15K','15-24K','25-34K','35-49K',
    '50-74K','75-99K','100-124K','125-149K',
    '150-174K','175-199K','200-249K','250K+'
]

plt.style.use('default')

# Validated two-series categorical palette (blue = no coupon, orange = coupon)
C_NO, C_YES = '#2a78d6', '#eb6834'
```

# Part 1: Your Visualization Toolkit {background="#2c3e50"}

## How Quickly Can You Spot Insights? {.smaller}

What can you tell from this [table]{style="color:steelblue;font-weight:bold;"}?

| Week | Produce | Dairy  | Frozen | Deli  |
|------|---------|--------|--------|-------|
| 1    | 11,500  | 12,100 | 7,320  | 4,100 |
| 2    | 12,800  | 11,400 | 7,180  | 4,080 |
| 3    | 12,200  | 10,800 | 1,780  | 4,120 |
| 4    | 13,900  | 10,100 | 7,410  | 4,090 |
| 5    | 13,400  | 9,800  | 7,260  | 4,110 |
| 6    | 15,100  | 9,200  | 7,350  | 4,085 |
| 7    | 14,800  | 8,700  | 7,420  | 4,115 |
| 8    | 16,400  | 8,100  | 7,190  | 4,095 |

## How Quickly Can You Spot Insights? {.smaller}

What can you tell from this [plot]{style="color:steelblue;font-weight:bold;"}?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5

data = {
    'Week': list(range(1, 9)) * 4,
    'Dept': ['Produce']*8 + ['Dairy']*8 + ['Frozen']*8 + ['Deli']*8,
    'Sales': [
        11500, 12800, 12200, 13900, 13400, 15100, 14800, 16400,  # Produce: upward trend
        12100, 11400, 10800, 10100,  9800,  9200,  8700,  8100,  # Dairy: downward trend
         7320,  7180,  1780,  7410,  7260,  7350,  7420,  7190,  # Frozen: stable + anomaly
         4100,  4080,  4120,  4090,  4110,  4085,  4115,  4095,  # Deli: flat
    ]
}
plot_df = pd.DataFrame(data)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
for dept, grp in plot_df.groupby('Dept'):
    ax.plot(grp['Week'], grp['Sales'], marker='o', label=dept, linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel('Week')
ax.set_ylabel('Weekly sales ($)')
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.StrMethodFormatter('{x:,.0f}'))
ax.legend(loc='center right')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Different Visualization Needs {.smaller}

::: {.callout}
## Scenario 1

You just pulled the Complete Journey data and need to quickly check whether basket spend looks reasonable before writing any analysis code.
:::

::: {.callout}
## Scenario 2

You're presenting weekly revenue trends to the VP of Marketing in a board meeting. The chart will appear in a formal slide deck.
:::

::: {.callout}
## Scenario 3

The promotions team wants a tool to interactively explore coupon redemption rates by store, product category, and week.
:::

. . .

**Same data. Three very different jobs.** No single library is best at all three.

## Match the Tool to the Goal {.smaller}

We should match ***how*** we visualize to the goal we have in mind.

<br>

| Purpose | Tool | Why It Wins Here |
|---------|------|-----------------|
| Quick EDA | **Pandas** `.plot()` | One line, straight off a DataFrame |
| Statistical comparison | **Seaborn** | Handles grouping, ordering, and stats for you |
| Polished reporting | **Matplotlib** | Total control over every element |
| Interactive exploration | **Bokeh** | Renders to the browser — zoom, hover, filter |

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
These are not four competitors. Pandas and Seaborn are both built **on top of** Matplotlib — so they stack.
:::

# Pandas: Speed {background="#43464B"}

## Pandas — When Speed Beats Polish {.smaller}

* Your **first reach** when you need a fast answer — minimal code, tied directly to DataFrames
* Call `.plot()` on any Series or DataFrame and pass `kind=`
* Built on Matplotlib, so anything you learn later still applies
* **Not** meant for final deliverables

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
If you can answer your question in one line, Pandas `.plot()` is the right tool. Rule of thumb: if you're typing a third line of formatting, you may want to switch libraries.
:::

## Pandas in One Line {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.5

category_totals.plot(
    kind='barh', x='department', y='sales_value',
    figsize=(10, 3.5), legend=False,
    title='Total revenue by department (top 10)', xlabel='Total sales ($)'
)
plt.show()
```

. . .

Swap `kind=` to change the chart: `'hist'`, `'box'`, `'line'`, `'bar'`, `'scatter'`, `'barh'`.

# Seaborn: Statistical Grouping {background="#43464B"}

## Seaborn — When You're Comparing Groups {.smaller}

* Built on Matplotlib — cleaner syntax for common **statistical** chart types
* Shines when you need **grouping, ordering, and distributions with shape**
* One function call handles what Matplotlib needs 10–15 lines to produce

. . .

<br>

| Pandas | Seaborn |
|--------|---------|
| `.plot(kind='hist')` — basic bin counts | `histplot()` — bins + KDE curve in one call |
| `.groupby().mean().plot.bar()` — manual aggregation | `boxplot()` / `barplot()` — handles stats automatically |
| No built-in group ordering | `order=` parameter on every chart |

. . .

Every Seaborn function follows one pattern: `sns.function(data=df, x=…, y=…, hue=…, order=…)`

## Seaborn in One Call {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| code-line-numbers: "2-9"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.8))
sns.boxplot(
    data=basket_demo,
    x='income',
    y='basket_spend',
    order=income_order,   # explicit ordering — critical for income brackets
    ax=ax,
    showfliers=False
)
ax.set_xticklabels(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel('Income bracket')
ax.set_ylabel('Basket spend ($)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Matplotlib: Control {background="#43464B"}

## Matplotlib — When the Chart Must Stand Alone {.smaller}

* The most widely used Python plotting library — and the **foundation** for Seaborn and Pandas
* **Full customization:** labels, annotations, tick formatting, styles, multi-panel layouts, export
* Because Pandas and Seaborn return Matplotlib objects, you can start fast and polish later

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
Use Matplotlib when the chart needs to stand on its own — in a report, a slide deck, or a published figure. **This is the library your project report will live on.**
:::

## The Figure / Axes Hierarchy {.smaller}

Everything in Matplotlib is an object you can reference and modify:

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.5

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.5))
# fig = the overall canvas
# ax  = the actual plot area (axes, ticks, lines, labels)
fig.set_facecolor('#eaf4fb')
ax.set_facecolor('#d0eaf8')
ax.set_title('fig (light blue canvas) contains ax (darker blue plot area)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

. . .

Once you have `fig` and `ax`, you control **everything** — including plots Seaborn or Pandas drew for you.

## Before: A Quick Pandas Plot {.smaller}

Fast, but it would not survive an executive meeting:

```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.0

weekly_sales.plot(kind='line', x='week', y='total_sales', figsize=(10, 3.0), legend=False)
plt.show()
```

## After: Executive-Ready Matplotlib {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-line-numbers: "|3-8|12-21"
#| output-location: slide

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.5))
ax.plot(weekly_sales['week'], weekly_sales['total_sales'], linewidth=2)

# --- readable formatting ---
ax.set_title('Weekly total sales — note holiday spike in late December', pad=10)
ax.set_xlabel('Week')
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.StrMethodFormatter('${x:,.0f}'))
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

# --- annotate the insight ---
peak_idx  = weekly_sales['total_sales'].idxmax()
peak_week = weekly_sales.loc[peak_idx, 'week']
peak_val  = weekly_sales.loc[peak_idx, 'total_sales']
ax.annotate(
    f'Holiday spike\n${peak_val:,.0f}',
    xy=(peak_week, peak_val),
    xytext=(peak_week - pd.Timedelta(weeks=8), peak_val * 0.97),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=1.2),
    fontsize=9
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-caution}
Matplotlib is powerful but verbose. There is a massive [example gallery](https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/index.html), and AI tools are very good at adapting Matplotlib code. The notebook walks this build step by step.
:::

# Bokeh: Interactivity {background="#43464B"}

## Bokeh — When Others Need to Explore {.smaller}

* Renders HTML/JavaScript — charts live in a **browser**, not just a notebook
* Users can **zoom, pan, hover, and filter** without writing new code
* Best for dashboards, stakeholder exploration tools, and shareable deliverables

```{python}
#| echo: false

from bokeh.plotting import figure, show
from bokeh.models import HoverTool, ColumnDataSource
from bokeh.io import output_notebook

output_notebook()
```

## Interactive Weekly Sales Explorer {.smaller .scrollable}

```{python}

source = ColumnDataSource(weekly_sales)

p = figure(
    title='Total Weekly Sales — hover, zoom, and pan to explore',
    x_axis_type='datetime',
    width=750, height=350,
    tools='pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save'
)

p.line('week', 'total_sales', source=source,
       line_width=2, color='steelblue')

hover = HoverTool(tooltips=[
    ('Week',  '@week{%F}'),
    ('Sales', '@total_sales{$0,0}')
], formatters={'@week': 'datetime'})
p.add_tools(hover)

p.xaxis.axis_label = 'Week'
p.yaxis.axis_label = 'Total Sales ($)'

show(p)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Run this in the companion notebook to see the interactive version — it won't fully render in a static slide.
:::

# Part 2: How to Think About EDA {background="#2c3e50"}

## You Already Have Most of What EDA Needs {.smaller}

| You learned | Which lets you |
|-------------|----------------|
| **Subsetting & filtering** (Wk 3) | isolate the rows a question is actually about |
| **`groupby` & aggregation** (Wk 4) | compute statistics at *any* level — household, basket, department, week |
| **Joins** (Wk 4) | pull in the context that makes a comparison possible |
| **Visualization** (this week) | see the shape, catch what's wrong, show the finding |

. . .

Aggregation tells you **what the numbers are**. Visualization tells you **what they mean** and helps you **communicate them**. Together, that is most of an EDA.

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
What's left is understanding how to **ask a good question of our data**.

That's what the rest of Part 2 is about.
:::

## EDA Is a Conversation With Your Data {.smaller}

Exploratory Data Analysis is not a checklist of charts to run.

It is a **sequence of questions** — each answer raising the next question.

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%'}
**Data dump (avoid)**

- Plot every variable
- Report every mean and median
- Move on

:::
::: {.column width='50%'}
**Real EDA (aim for)**

- Start with a sharp question
- Let findings drive the next step
- Stop when you can tell a story
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
The goal is not to show that you looked at the data. The goal is to find something worth saying.
:::

## A Framework for EDA {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
    A["1️⃣ Question"] --> B["2️⃣ Structure"]
    B --> C["3️⃣ Distributions"]
    C --> D["4️⃣ Segmentation"]
    D --> E["5️⃣ Story"]
    style A fill:#2c3e50,color:#fff
    style B fill:#2980b9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#27ae60,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e67e22,color:#fff
    style E fill:#8e44ad,color:#fff
```

<br>

| Step | Question to ask |
|------|----------------|
| **Question** | What do I actually want to know? Is it specific enough to know when I've answered it? |
| **Structure** | What shape is the data? What do I need to join? Where are the missing values? |
| **Distributions** | What does the outcome variable look like across all households? Any outliers? |
| **Segmentation** | Does the pattern differ across groups? Where does the interesting variation live? |
| **Story** | What changed? What surprised me? What should the decision-maker do next? |

## Step 1: Start With a Sharp Question {.smaller}

The question determines everything that follows.

. . .

::: {.callout-caution}
**Too broad:** "How do customers shop?"

This can't be answered — no unit of analysis, no metric, no comparison to make.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
**Sharp:** "Do households that redeem coupons have larger basket spend than those that don't — and does this differ across income brackets?"

This names: the unit (basket), the metric (spend), the comparison (coupon vs. no coupon), and the segmentation (income).
:::

. . .

A sharp EDA question tells you which tables to join, which columns to compute, and what a result would look like.

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
**We are going to answer this exact question** over the next four slides — one step of the framework at a time.
:::

## Step 2: Structure — What Do I Actually Have? {.smaller}

Our question compares **baskets**, but `transactions` gives us 1.5 million *item* rows. So the first move is structural: collapse to **one row per basket**, flag which ones used a coupon, then attach household demographics for the income half of the question.

Every one of those steps can quietly lose rows — so count what survives:

```{python}
#| echo: false

n_baskets   = len(baskets)
n_coupon    = int(baskets['used_coupon'].sum())
pct_coupon  = 100 * baskets['used_coupon'].mean()
n_joined    = len(baskets_demo)
pct_kept    = 100 * n_joined / n_baskets

print(f"Baskets:                    {n_baskets:,}")
print(f"  ... that used a coupon:   {n_coupon:,}  ({pct_coupon:.1f}%)")
print(f"Households:                 {baskets['household_id'].nunique():,}")
print()
print(f"After joining demographics: {n_joined:,} baskets  ({pct_kept:.0f}% kept)")
print(f"  ... households:           {baskets_demo['household_id'].nunique():,}")
```

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
**The join cost us half the data.** Only 801 households have demographics. Any income comparison we make describes *those* households — not all shoppers. Notice this now, not in your conclusion.
:::

## Step 3: Distributions — Which Summary Can I Trust? {.smaller .scrollable}

Before comparing any groups, look at the outcome variable alone: **what does a typical basket even look like?**

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.0))
sns.histplot(data=baskets, x='basket_spend', bins=60, kde=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlim(0, 120)
ax.axvline(baskets['basket_spend'].mean(),   color='crimson', ls='--', lw=1.6,
           label=f"mean  ${baskets['basket_spend'].mean():.2f}")
ax.axvline(baskets['basket_spend'].median(), color='seagreen', ls='-',  lw=1.6,
           label=f"median ${baskets['basket_spend'].median():.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel('Basket spend ($)')
ax.set_title(f"Basket spend is heavily right-skewed (skew = {baskets['basket_spend'].skew():.1f})")
ax.legend()
for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

. . .

The mean sits **$12 above** the median — a handful of enormous baskets drag it to the right.

::: {.callout-important}
## Report the median — and say why you did

With skew this strong, the **mean describes a basket almost nobody actually has**. The median is what a typical trip looks like, and it barely moves when a few $300 stock-ups show up.

Put that reasoning in your own report — one sentence is enough: *“We compare medians because basket spend is right-skewed.”* It tells your reader the choice was deliberate rather than a default, and defending a judgment call like this is exactly what the EDA portion of the rubric rewards.
:::

## Step 4: Segmentation — Does the Pattern Hold? {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2

med = baskets.groupby('used_coupon')['basket_spend'].median()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.2))
bars = ax.bar(['No coupon', 'Used a coupon'], [med[False], med[True]],
              color=[C_NO, C_YES], width=0.5)
for b, v in zip(bars, [med[False], med[True]]):
    ax.text(b.get_x()+b.get_width()/2, v+1.2, f'${v:,.2f}', ha='center', fontsize=11, weight='bold')
ax.set_ylabel('Median basket spend ($)')
ax.set_title('Coupon baskets are 3.3x larger')
ax.set_ylim(0, 62)
for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

. . .

**And across income brackets?** The lift shows up in *every* bracket — 100% to 290%, with no clean upward or downward pattern.

::: {.callout-note}
Let's look, rather than assert.
:::

## Step 4 (cont.): Does It Differ by Income? {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6

import numpy as np

med = (baskets_demo.groupby(['income', 'used_coupon'])['basket_spend']
       .median().unstack().reindex(income_order))
hh  = baskets_demo.groupby('income')['household_id'].nunique().reindex(income_order)

x, w = np.arange(len(income_order)), 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))

# thin-data band behind the last three brackets
ax.axvspan(x[-3] - 0.5, x[-1] + 0.5, color='#f0eeea', zorder=0)

ax.bar(x - w/2 - 0.01, med[False], w, label='No coupon',     color=C_NO,  zorder=3)
ax.bar(x + w/2 + 0.01, med[True],  w, label='Used a coupon', color=C_YES, zorder=3)

ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(income_order, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel('Median basket spend ($)')
ax.set_title('Spend rises with income — but the coupon gap holds at every level')
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.StrMethodFormatter('${x:,.0f}'))
ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.25, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc='upper left', frameon=False, fontsize=9)
ax.text(x[-2], ax.get_ylim()[1]*0.90,
        f'only {hh.iloc[-3:].min()}–{hh.iloc[-3:].max()} households',
        ha='center', fontsize=8, color='#6b6b66', style='italic', zorder=4)
for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

. . .

Orange clears blue in **every single bracket**. Both series drift up with income — so the real question is whether the *gap* widens.

::: {.callout-note}
It doesn't. As a ratio the lift bounces from **roughly 100% up to 290%** with no clean direction. Richer households spend more per trip, coupon or not — but **the coupon effect itself is not an income story.** The second half of our question resolves to "no," and ruling something out is progress, not failure.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
And notice the shaded brackets: those medians rest on **5–11 households**. That is the Step 2 join loss surfacing exactly where you'd be most tempted to read a trend.
:::

## Step 5: Build the Story — and the "So What" Test {.smaller}

A 3.3x gap is tempting. **Push one question further before you recommend anything.**

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9

g = baskets.groupby('used_coupon')
lines, per_line = g['n_lines'].median(), g['spend_per_line'].median()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 2.9))
labels = ['No coupon', 'Coupon']

axes[0].bar(labels, [lines[False], lines[True]], color=[C_NO, C_YES], width=0.5)
axes[0].set_title('Median items per basket')
for i, v in enumerate([lines[False], lines[True]]):
    axes[0].text(i, v+0.5, f'{v:.0f}', ha='center', weight='bold')
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 23)

axes[1].bar(labels, [per_line[False], per_line[True]], color=[C_NO, C_YES], width=0.5)
axes[1].set_title('Median spend per item')
for i, v in enumerate([per_line[False], per_line[True]]):
    axes[1].text(i, v+0.08, f'${v:.2f}', ha='center', weight='bold')
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 3.6)

for ax in axes:
    for spine in ['top', 'right']:
        ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

. . .

**Spend per item is identical.** Coupon baskets are not *pricier* — they are simply **bigger trips**.

## What We Can — and Cannot — Say {.smaller}

::: {.callout-important}
## The "So What" Test

*So what?* Coupon redemption marks the **weekly stock-up trip**, not a change in what people buy.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-caution}
**The recommendation we cannot make:** *"Send more coupons to grow basket size."*

Nothing here shows coupons **caused** bigger baskets. Shoppers planning a big trip may be the ones who bother to bring a coupon. 
:::

. . .

<br>

**Next question:** do the *same* households shop differently with and without a coupon? That comparison could support a causal claim. This one can't.

---

# Part 3: The Midterm Project {background="#2c3e50"}

## The Regork Scenario {.smaller}

You are a data scientist at **Regork**, a national grocery chain.

Your manager has asked you to identify a **potential growth opportunity** — an area where the company could invest future resources to increase revenue or profits.

. . .

Your task:

1. Define a **clear business question** that investigates a specific growth opportunity
2. Analyze the Complete Journey data to answer it
3. Communicate your findings through:
   - A **written analytic report** (Jupyter Notebook → HTML)
   - A **3-minute recorded presentation** for the CEO

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
**Groups:** 2–4 students. Join one of the pre-defined groups in Canvas → People → Mid-Term Project. You may not create your own group outside that list.
:::

## What a Sharp Business Question Looks Like {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip}
## You just watched one get answered

*"Do households that redeem coupons have larger basket spend than those that don't — and does this differ across income brackets?"*
:::

That question survived contact with the data because it named four things up front:

| It named | Which told us |
|----------|---------------|
| A **unit** — the basket | what one row of our table had to be |
| A **metric** — spend | what to compute, and that skew mattered |
| A **comparison** — coupon vs. not | what the chart at Step 4 had to show |
| A **segmentation** — income | what to check next, even though it came back empty |

. . .

Notice it was answerable in **four steps** — and we knew we were done. That is the bar.

## Three More Sharp Questions {.smaller .scrollable}

<br>

::: {.callout-tip}
## Private label

*“Do households with kids buy a higher share of private-label products than households without — and does that gap differ by department?”*

Unit: household · Metric: private-label share of spend · Compare: kids vs. none · Segment: department
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Trip behavior

*“Do households that shop twice a week or more spend more over the year than occasional shoppers — or do they spread the same annual spend across more trips?”*

Unit: household · Metric: annual spend & trip count · Compare: frequent vs. occasional · Segment: income
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Promotions

*“Do products featured in the weekly mailer sell more during the featured week — and does any lift carry into the week after?”*

Unit: product-week · Metric: units sold · Compare: featured vs. not · Segment: department
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
Notice the second one has the **same shape as our coupon finding**: *“more spend”* and *“more trips”* are different answers, and the question is built so you can tell them apart. Design that distinction in from the start — don't discover it at the end.
:::

## What Strong Analysis Looks Like {.smaller}

::: incremental
**A question worth asking** — specific, answerable, and tied to a decision someone actually makes. You saw the standard in Part 2.

**A named decision-maker** — who acts on this, and what do they do differently on Monday? The VP of Promotions needs a recommendation, not a summary of what you computed.

**Reasoning you can follow** — structure, then distributions, then segmentation. Each step raises the next question. Show the reasoning, not just the outputs.

**Honesty about limits** — say what your analysis does *not* establish. The strongest projects name the recommendation they can't yet make, and what would be needed to make it.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
Every chart earns its place by making **one** point. Label the axes, use a readable scale, and narrate what the reader should see. Plots without interpretation are decoration.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Don't guess at the bar — go look at it

The Canvas project page includes **real report and presentation submissions from previous classes.** They are the clearest picture you will get of what “strong” actually means.

Before you write anything, read two of them end to end and ask: *what did they investigate, how did they narrate each chart, and where did they choose to stop?* An hour spent there will do more for your grade than an extra hour of code.
:::
